Baby & Child

A wart on a child’s hand or foot: wait or treat?

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Your school-age child takes off a football boot and shows you a tender patch under the heel. Their brother has a rough wart on a finger that hardly bothers him. If the spots are warts, the two children may still choose different plans. Pain when walking, changes in the skin and what matters to the child are useful places to start.

Look at what the wart is getting in the way of

A common wart often feels rough and may interrupt the usual skin lines on a finger or knuckle. A plantar wart grows on the sole. Pressure from walking can push it inward and make standing uncomfortable. Several plantar warts can grow together in a cluster. Tiny dark dots can be small blood vessels. A corn, callus or another growth can also feel hard underfoot.

Ask your child when they notice it most. Does it hurt on the way to school, catch on a pencil or simply look different? A clinician can usually identify a wart by examination. Ask for a check if you are unsure, if an area bleeds or changes, or if a sore foot changes how the child walks. Do not cut into it to find out what it is.

Waiting can be a reasonable choice

For a confirmed wart that does not hurt or get in the way, ask whether observation makes sense. The immune system often clears common warts over time. Some disappear within months, while others persist for years or come back after treatment. Agree on a reason to revisit the choice, such as pain, spreading lesions or a change in appearance.

Ask how your child feels about being treated. A child who is bothered by classmates asking about a finger may want help; one with a painless wart might prefer to leave it alone. A dermatologist can help if there are many lesions, persistent pain or uncertainty. A wart on the face or genitals, or warts in a child with a weakened immune system, should be assessed before any home treatment.

Treatment depends on the site

For an older child with a confirmed common or plantar wart, ask a clinician or pharmacist if a salicylic-acid wart product is appropriate for the child’s age and the particular spot. Follow the directions for that product, protect nearby skin and stop and seek advice if it becomes very sore. Never put a hand or foot wart product on the face, genitals, broken or infected skin. Do not start home treatment if the child has diabetes or impaired circulation without medical advice.

Freezing with liquid nitrogen in a clinic can hurt, can leave a blister and may need repeat visits. In a trial of 250 people aged four to 79, freezing cleared more common warts at 13 weeks than acid or waiting. For plantar warts, the researchers found no clinically relevant difference among the three approaches at that point. The study included adults as well as children and does not predict the outcome for one sore heel. Ask what benefit to expect and when to reassess.

Reduce spread without making the child sit out

The types of human papillomavirus that cause common warts enter through small breaks in the skin. Touching a wart, picking around it or biting the skin around the nails can give the virus a route to another site. Someone else can also acquire it through contact or a shared personal item. You normally cannot trace a wart to one classmate or outing.

Wash hands after touching a wart. Give each child their own towel and nail clippers, and choose footwear for communal showers or wet changing areas. Cover the wart if needed for an activity and follow the facility’s rules. Ordinary school attendance can continue. Help the child name their practical concern to an adult, such as needing a break because a shoe presses on the sore spot.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Base the decision to treat on an examination, symptoms, location and the child’s priorities.

Check age and site restrictions before putting any wart medicine on a child’s skin.

Review a painful, bleeding, changing or uncertain lesion and seek advice for warts in a child with impaired immunity.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests asking how the spot affects holding a pencil, walking or putting on a shoe. The answer can help the family and clinician decide what improvement is worth the discomfort or time of treatment.

When to seek help

Have uncertain, rapidly changing, bleeding or painful growths assessed. Seek prompt advice for pus or spreading redness, especially if the child has a fever or seems unwell. Avoid wart remover on the face or genitals.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Childhood warts, when to see a clinician and prevention
  • American Academy of Dermatology — Diagnosis and treatment of common and plantar warts
  • Bruggink and colleagues, CMAJ — Trial comparing freezing, salicylic acid and observation for warts
  • American Academy of Dermatology — Practical ways to reduce the spread of warts

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A painful spot on the sole may need examination, especially if a child is changing how they walk.
  • A confirmed painless wart can often be observed. Ask about an age-appropriate treatment if it interferes with daily activities.
  • Avoid picking, use separate towels and wear shoes in shared wet areas.

Frequently asked questions

Can a wart on a child’s hand spread?

Yes. Skin contact, picking and some shared items can spread the virus to another area or another person. Wash hands after contact, avoid biting at a wart and use separate nail tools.

What causes a plantar wart?

Certain types of HPV can infect the skin through tiny breaks on the sole. The pressure of standing can make the wart grow inward and hurt. A clinician can distinguish it from other causes of a tender patch.

Which children are more likely to get warts?

They are common in school-age children. Small cuts, nail biting and contact with the virus can provide opportunities for infection. A weakened immune system can make warts harder to clear. Getting one is not a measure of how clean a child is.

How long will treatment take?

Topical treatment often takes weeks of regular use; freezing may take several visits. Timing varies with the site, size, treatment and response. Ask when to stop or have the diagnosis reviewed if it is not improving. New or recurrent warts are possible.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
